title: How Lobotomies Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how lobotomies work, tracing the history from early 1930s shock therapies (insulin, Metrazol, electroconvulsive therapy) through the 1935 prefrontal lobotomy developed by Antonio Egas Moniz and Almeida Lima in Portugal, based on Yale monkey research, to Walter Freeman's rapid transorbital "ice pick" lobotomy in the US. They cover the prefrontal cortex and gray/white matter, the estimated tens of thousands of US lobotomies, Freeman's showmanship and fatal incidents, notable cases including Rosemary Kennedy and Howard Dully, why the procedure fell out of use after chlorpromazine (Thorazine) in 1950, and that psychosurgery still occurs in England. The episode includes an ad for Audible and a listener mail segment about nature and man-made compounds.

segments.title: Pre-lobotomy treatments of the 1930s
segments.summary: Overview of mental institutions in the 1930s and convulsive treatments: insulin shock, Metrazol-induced convulsions, and electroconvulsive therapy, based on a supposed link between epilepsy and mental illness.

segments.title: Origins of the lobotomy: Moniz and the Yale monkey study
segments.summary: Overcrowded mental hospitals and the lack of drug therapy set the stage. Moniz and Lima in Portugal performed the first lobotomies by drilling into the skull and injecting alcohol, inspired by a 1935 Yale study in which monkeys lost prefrontal cortex and showed reduced emotion.

segments.title: How the brain's prefrontal cortex and white matter work
segments.summary: Explanation of the prefrontal cortex's executive functions and personality, the difference between gray and white matter, and how lobotomy aims to sever white matter connections. Moniz's alcohol technique spread too widely, so he refined the drilling method and used an instrument to remove tissue.

segments.title: Walter Freeman and the transorbital ice pick lobotomy
segments.summary: Walter Freeman, a neurologist, sought a faster method than surgery. He developed the transorbital ice pick lobotomy, inserting an instrument above the eyeball and tapping it through the orbital bone, performed without anesthesia after electroshock. Freeman's speed, showmanship on his lobotomobile tour, and the varied outcomes are described.

segments.title: Deaths, criticism and notable patients
segments.summary: Freeman's dangerous showmanship led to a fatal accident in Iowa. Soviet Union banned lobotomies. Rosemary Kennedy was lobotomized, and Howard Dully's case, including his stepmother's complaints and his later radio piece, is recounted.

segments.title: Decline of lobotomy and modern psychosurgery
segments.summary: Lobotomies fell out of use due to criticism involving criminals and soldiers and the arrival of Thorazine in 1950. Freeman's last lobotomy in 1967 led to a ban on his surgery, and psychosurgery continues in England today.

segments.title: Listener mail on nature and man-made compounds
segments.summary: A listener writes that man-made chemicals like fruit dose and corn syrup are part of nature, since man is part of nature, quoting Alan Watts. Hosts thank him.
